faqs.q: What should a CAM reconciliation statement template include?
faqs.a: A complete CAM reconciliation statement template includes: a header with property name, tenant name, lease reference, and reconciliation period; a recoverable expense summary with GL codes and exclusions; a gross-up calculation section; a pro-rata share calculation; a CAM cap comparison; estimated payment summary; and the final true-up balance.

faqs.q: Can I use this template with data from Yardi or MRI?
faqs.a: Yes. Export your GL report as a CSV or Excel from Yardi, MRI, AppFolio, or any ERP, then paste the expense totals into the template. CapVeri's online reconciliation generator also accepts GL exports directly for fully automated calculation.

faqs.q: Is this template compliant with SB 1103 in California?
faqs.a: The template includes California SB 1103 disclosure support for eligible commercial leases, with expense line item formatting and allocation-basis documentation fields for customer and counsel review.

faqs.q: What formulas are included in the CAM reconciliation Excel template?
faqs.a: The template includes pre-built formulas for: pro-rata share calculation (tenant SF / denominator SF), gross-up (variable expenses / actual occupancy % x threshold %), cumulative CAM cap with carry-forward logic, non-cumulative cap ceiling calculation, and true-up (annual obligation minus estimated payments received).

faqs.q: How many tenants does the Excel template support?
faqs.a: The standard template supports up to 20 tenants. Each tenant has a row in the tenant roster tab with their leased SF, denominator definition, gross-up threshold, and cap percentage. For larger portfolios, CapVeri's software handles unlimited tenants from a single GL import.

faqs.q: Can I calculate CAM reconciliation in Excel?
faqs.a: Yes. Excel is the most common tool for CAM reconciliation at small to mid-size portfolios. The main risks are formula errors (especially in gross-up and cap calculations) and manual data entry mistakes from copying GL data. CapVeri's automated reconciliation eliminates these risks by importing GL data directly.

faqs.q: What should be on a CAM reconciliation checklist?
faqs.a: A complete CAM reconciliation checklist should cover: (1) data gathering: GL export, lease abstracts, rent roll, and prior year reconciliation; (2) expense review: categorization, exclusions, gross-up calculation; (3) calculations: pro-rata share and cap verification; (4) statement preparation: formatting and disclosure fields; (5) tenant delivery: timing, method, and certified mail if required; (6) payment tracking: true-up collection and credit issuance.

faqs.q: When should a CAM reconciliation be completed?
faqs.a: Most commercial leases require CAM reconciliation within 90-120 days after the fiscal year end. For calendar-year leases, the reconciliation is typically due by March 31 or April 30 of the following year. Some leases specify shorter windows. Always verify the exact deadline in the lease.

faqs.q: How do I use a CAM reconciliation checklist?
faqs.a: Work through the checklist sequentially before, during, and after the reconciliation process. Start with data gathering (GL export, lease abstracts, prior year reconciliation), then move through expense categorization, calculation verification (gross-up, pro-rata, caps), and finally statement preparation and delivery. Check off each item as completed and note any items that need follow-up.

faqs.q: What should a tenant CAM reconciliation letter include?
faqs.a: A tenant CAM reconciliation letter should include: the reconciliation period, a summary of total actual expenses vs. the tenant's estimated payments, the net true-up amount (balance due or credit), a clear payment due date, the method for requesting a copy of supporting records, tenant audit rights and the audit request deadline, and landlord contact information.

faqs.q: How should a landlord send a CAM reconciliation letter?
faqs.a: Most leases specify the required delivery method, typically certified mail or email to the address in the lease notice provisions. For California leases subject to SB 1103, delivery method and timing requirements are more specific. Always verify the lease's notice provisions before sending.

faqs.q: Does a tenant have the right to audit CAM charges?
faqs.a: Most commercial leases grant tenants an audit right, typically a window of 12-36 months from receiving the reconciliation statement. Some states have statutory audit rights regardless of lease language. The reconciliation letter should reference the applicable audit rights and deadlines.

faqs.q: What CAM disclosure does SB 1103 require in California?
faqs.a: SB 1103 requires landlords to provide qualified small business tenants with an itemized list of actual operating expenses by category, the basis for allocating expenses, and documentation of how the tenant's pro-rata share was calculated. The reconciliation statement must be sent within 90 days after the fiscal year end.

faqs.q: Which leases are subject to SB 1103 in California?
faqs.a: SB 1103 applies to new commercial leases entered on or after January 1, 2025 with 'qualified commercial tenants' - primarily small businesses with fewer than 5 employees and monthly gross receipts under $2.5 million, as well as microenterprise and nonprofit tenants meeting specific criteria.

faqs.q: Does Texas have specific CAM reconciliation requirements?
faqs.a: Texas does not have a statute governing CAM reconciliation timing or disclosure requirements like California's SB 1103. CAM rights and obligations are governed entirely by the lease agreement. However, HCAD property tax dynamics (ARB protests, assessment adjustments) significantly affect property tax recovery in Texas and require specific handling in the reconciliation.

faqs.q: How does an HCAD ARB protest affect CAM charges?
faqs.a: If a landlord wins a property tax protest through HCAD's Appraisal Review Board, the resulting tax savings affect the CAM pool. The HCAD Tax Normalizer helps landlords calculate the exact additional recovery they can bill to tenants based on the ARB outcome and any applicable lease caps.

faqs.q: Are CAM caps common in Florida commercial leases?
faqs.a: Yes. Non-cumulative CAM caps (typically 3-5%) are common in Florida retail and strip center NNN leases. The cap limits year-over-year increases in tenant CAM obligations regardless of actual expense growth. Florida's high insurance costs and occasional hurricane impacts can drive expense spikes that make cap provisions particularly significant.

faqs.q: Does Florida have specific CAM reconciliation laws?
faqs.a: Florida does not have a general statute governing CAM reconciliation requirements for commercial leases. The rights and obligations are lease-driven. However, Florida landlords must comply with general property law requirements and any specific provisions in the lease regarding notice, audit rights, and reconciliation timing.

faqs.q: Do NNN leases require annual reconciliation?
faqs.a: Yes. Triple net leases require annual reconciliation because tenants pay estimated monthly amounts throughout the year. At year-end, actual property taxes, insurance premiums, and operating expenses are compared to estimates, and the difference is reconciled as a true-up payment or credit.

faqs.q: What's the difference between NNN and NN reconciliation?
faqs.a: In a triple net (NNN) lease, tenants are responsible for all three pass-throughs: property taxes, insurance, and CAM. In a double net (NN) lease, tenants pay property taxes and insurance, but the landlord typically covers CAM. The reconciliation scope differs accordingly: NNN reconciliations include all three categories, NN reconciliations typically cover only taxes and insurance.

faqs.q: How should a landlord respond to a tenant CAM dispute?
faqs.a: A landlord should respond to a CAM dispute in writing within the timeframe specified in the lease. The response should: acknowledge receipt of the dispute, address each disputed item with a specific explanation and supporting documentation reference, offer to provide the GL detail and invoices the tenant is entitled to under the audit clause, and state a clear resolution timeline.

faqs.q: What documentation should a landlord provide in a CAM dispute?
faqs.a: In a CAM dispute, landlords should be prepared to provide: the full GL expense detail for the reconciliation period, invoices for significant expense items, the lease abstract showing the reconciliation methodology, prior year reconciliation comparisons, and documentation of any gross-up calculations or cap applications.

faqs.q: When must a landlord send the annual CAM estimate letter?
faqs.a: Most leases require the landlord to send the annual CAM estimate letter at least 30-60 days before the start of the new lease year. The letter sets the new monthly CAM payment amount for the upcoming year. Check the lease's specific notice requirements. Some leases allow landlords to continue charging the prior year's estimate until a new letter is sent.

faqs.q: How is the CAM estimate calculated?
faqs.a: The CAM estimate is typically calculated by taking the prior year's actual recoverable expenses, adding a projected increase based on known or expected expense changes (CPI, contract renewals, etc.), and dividing by 12 to get the monthly estimate. The estimate should reflect a reasonable projection of actual expenses to minimize large true-ups.
